items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care practice standard and Code of Conduct 3.13; Ontario professional misconduct regulation referenced in the standard.
items.stem: An Ontario client in independent nursing practice asks to discontinue nursing services. According to CNO accountabilities, which action is required?

options.text: Arrange timely alternative or replacement services, or give the client a reasonable opportunity to arrange alternative services
Stop all contact immediately without arranging or allowing time for alternative care
Refuse the client’s request and continue visits indefinitely regardless of the client’s wishes
Transfer the client’s health records to social media so the public can find another nurse

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Code of Conduct 3.13 and the Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care standard: when services are discontinued at the client’s request, nurses arrange timely alternative or replacement services or provide a reasonable opportunity to arrange alternatives. Professional misconduct rules likewise require alternatives or a reasonable opportunity unless the client requests discontinuation (which still requires ensuring ongoing access).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Abrupt cessation without arranging alternatives or a reasonable opportunity abandons needed care and conflicts with CNO continuity accountabilities.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Capable clients may request discontinuation; nurses must respect the request while ensuring ongoing access pathways (CNO).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Sharing PHI on social media violates privacy and is not an alternative-care arrangement.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships practice standard (updated Dec 2025 / in effect Mar 1, 2026).
items.stem: A home-care client asks the nurse to borrow $50 until the next pension cheque. Which response best upholds professional boundaries?

options.text: Decline financial transactions unrelated to care (do not lend or borrow money) and, if needed, refer the client to appropriate resources
Lend the money from personal funds because the amount is small and the client seems trustworthy
Ask the client to add the nurse as a joint bank-account holder to ‘help manage bills’
Accept a larger cash ‘gift’ from the client in exchange for the loan

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Professional Boundaries: nurses must not engage in financial transactions unrelated to care with a client or family (e.g., borrowing money). OpenStax: social boundaries require avoiding nontherapeutic socialization/personal entanglement; keep the focus on the client’s care needs and refer appropriately.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lending money is a prohibited financial transaction outside care (CNO).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Joint finances create a major boundary violation and conflict of interest (CNO).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Exchanging gifts/money for personal benefit blurs boundaries and risks misconduct (CNO).

items.stem: A nurse slept only 3 hours before a busy shift and feels less sharp than usual. Using the TeamSTEPPS I’M SAFE checklist, which action best supports situation monitoring?

options.text: Alert the team about fatigue (for example, ask colleagues to watch more closely today) so the team can support safe performance
Hide the fatigue and refuse any help so no one questions competence
Drink alcohol before the shift to ‘relax into the workload’
Skip handoffs entirely to conserve energy

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ I’M SAFE: Fatigue — team members should alert the team (e.g., “Watch me a little closer today. I only had 3 hours of sleep last night.”). Situation monitoring supports shared awareness so the team can compensate. OpenStax lists situation monitoring among TeamSTEPPS core competencies.
rationales.B: Incorrect. I’M SAFE expects honest awareness and disclosure of factors that impair safety, not concealment.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Alcohol/drugs is an I’M SAFE risk factor that impairs focus; using alcohol worsens safety.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Skipping handoffs removes critical communication and increases risk.

items.stem: A charge nurse teaches situation monitoring using the TeamSTEPPS STEP tool. Complete the teaching statement.

ngn.template: STEP prompts teams to monitor the {B1} (including vitals and care plan), the status of {B2} (including fatigue and workload), the {B3} (staffing, equipment, acuity), and {B4} toward established goals so the plan can be revised when needed.

B3.text: colour of the break-room walls only

rationales.B1a: Correct. AHRQ STEP monitors patient status (history, vitals, medications, exam, care plan, psychosocial factors).
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Vendor stock prices are not a STEP patient-status element.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Social media metrics are unrelated to clinical situation monitoring.
rationales.B2a: Correct. AHRQ STEP includes awareness of team members (fatigue, workload, task performance, skill, stress).
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Celebrity status is not a TeamSTEPPS team-member element.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. STEP focuses on the working team’s current functioning, not only off-duty staff.
rationales.B3a: Correct. AHRQ STEP assesses environment (occupancy, staffing, triage acuity, outbreaks, equipment).
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Decorative wall colour alone is not the environmental monitoring intent.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Parking fines are unrelated to care-environment monitoring.
rationales.B4a: Correct. AHRQ STEP monitors progress toward goals so the plan can be revised or resources added.
rationales.B4b: Incorrect. Punitive silence is not a STEP element.
rationales.B4c: Incorrect. Withholding concerns opposes TeamSTEPPS safety culture.

items.stem: A community health nurse teaches adults how to prevent hepatitis B virus infection. Which statement is the priority prevention teaching point?

options.text: Getting vaccinated is the best way to prevent hepatitis B
Isolation of infected persons is the primary community prevention strategy because vaccine adds little
Hepatitis B is mainly spread by casual hugging and sharing utensils, so avoid all social contact
There is no vaccine; only herbal teas prevent infection

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: the best way to prevent hepatitis B is vaccination. Merck: routine HepB vaccination is recommended to prevent infection; vaccination in endemic areas has dramatically reduced prevalence.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck notes isolation of patients is of no value for HBV prevention; vaccination and risk-behaviour counselling are the focus.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC: HBV is not spread by hugging, sneezing, coughing, or sharing utensils; it spreads via blood and certain body fluids.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Safe, effective HepB vaccines exist and are recommended (CDC/Merck).

items.stem: A pregnant client at 28 weeks’ gestation asks about whooping cough (pertussis) protection for the newborn. Which teaching is appropriate?

options.text: Receive one Tdap dose during every pregnancy, preferably early in weeks 27 through 36
Skip Tdap in pregnancy if a dose was given 2 years ago for a tetanus booster
Tdap is never given in pregnancy; wait until the child is 5 years old
Only the newborn needs vaccination at birth for pertussis; maternal Tdap is unnecessary

rationales.A: Correct. CDC and Merck: give a single Tdap during every pregnancy, preferably in the early part of gestational weeks 27–36, regardless of the interval since prior Tdap.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Additional Tdap is recommended each pregnancy regardless of interval since the previous dose (CDC/Merck).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Tdap in pregnancy is specifically recommended to protect infants (CDC/Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Maternal vaccination in pregnancy is recommended to transfer antibodies; infants begin DTaP later in infancy, not a birth pertussis dose as the sole strategy.

items.stem: A client begins to disclose a painful personal experience. The nurse feels uncomfortable and quickly asks about the weather instead. Which evaluation of this response is accurate?

options.text: Changing the subject is a nontherapeutic barrier that can seem insensitive and shut down disclosure
Changing the subject is the preferred therapeutic technique for painful topics
Changing the subject always increases trust more than active listening
Nurses should change the subject whenever clients show emotion

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax PMH: changing the subject dismisses important disclosure and can seem uncaring; use active listening instead. OpenStax Fundamentals: changing the subject is listed among nontherapeutic techniques.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Changing the subject is classified as nontherapeutic, not preferred therapy.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Active listening supports trust; changing the subject undermines it.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Emotional disclosure is a cue to stay present therapeutically, not to divert.

items.stem: For each nursing response, indicate whether it is a barrier to therapeutic communication (Avoid) or a therapeutic approach (Use).

rows.text: Providing false reassurance that is not based on facts
Changing the subject when the client discloses something painful
Using active listening and clarifying questions to keep the message flowing
Minimizing the client’s concern (for example, ‘it could be worse’)

rationales.R1: Avoid (barrier). OpenStax lists providing false reassurances among barriers/nontherapeutic techniques.
rationales.R2: Avoid (barrier). Changing the subject is a listed barrier/nontherapeutic technique.
rationales.R3: Use (therapeutic). OpenStax: instead of changing the subject, use active listening and clarifying questions.
rationales.R4: Avoid (barrier). Minimizing remarks (e.g., ‘it could be worse’) are nontherapeutic barriers.

items.stem: A client with schizophrenia firmly believes hospital food is poisoned despite evidence to the contrary. After safety is assured, which nursing communication approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Establish trust with therapeutic communication, then help the client focus on reality-based themes rather than arguing about the delusion
Agree that the food is poisoned to build rapport
Loudly argue until the client retracts the belief
Ignore the client and withhold all meals indefinitely

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: for clients experiencing delusions, establish therapeutic communication and trust, then help focus on reality-based themes. Merck: delusions are erroneous beliefs maintained despite clear contradictory evidence — arguing facts alone rarely erases the belief; supportive, reality-oriented psychosocial care is part of treatment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Reinforcing a delusion is not therapeutic and can worsen safety planning.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Confrontational arguing is nontherapeutic and may escalate distress.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Withholding meals is harmful and unrelated to therapeutic communication.

items.stem: A 5-week-old infant has forceful, nonbilious vomiting after feeds, still seems hungry, and has a firm olive-like mass in the right epigastrium. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Uncomplicated physiologic gastroesophageal reflux with bilious emesis only
Typical viral gastroenteritis with predominantly watery diarrhea and no vomiting
Simple overfeeding without gastric outlet obstruction risk

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis typically presents at 3–6 weeks with forceful/projectile nonbilious emesis after eating; an olive-like pyloric mass may be palpable. NCBI StatPearls physiology text: IHPS presents with projectile nonbilious vomiting and a palpable olive; definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy after fluid/electrolyte correction.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Classic pyloric stenosis emesis is nonbilious; bilious vomiting suggests a different obstruction pattern.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The vignette centres on postprandial projectile vomiting and an olive mass, not diarrhea-predominant gastroenteritis.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting with an olive mass indicates gastric outlet obstruction needing evaluation, not simple overfeeding.

items.stem: A public health nurse teaches daycare staff how to limit spread of hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wash hands often with soap and water, especially after diaper changes and toileting
Clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces and shared toys
Avoid close contact such as hugging or kissing persons who are infected
Rely on a routinely available HFMD vaccine in Canada/US as the primary prevention method
Avoid contact with open skin lesions and oral secretions (drool) when caring for ill children

rationales.A: Correct. CDC and Merck emphasize meticulous hand hygiene, especially around diaper changes/stooling.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC: clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces and shared items including toys.
rationales.C: Correct. CDC: avoid close contact with infected persons (hugging/kissing).
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC: no HFMD vaccine in the United States; Merck: EV-A71 vaccines exist in China but none approved in the US.
rationales.E: Correct. Merck: avoid contact with open skin lesions and oral secretions to limit spread; CDC notes spread via blister fluid.

items.stem: A 4-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, remains eager to feed, and has a palpable olive-like epigastric mass. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

actions.text: Support airway/breathing as needed and keep NPO pending surgical evaluation
Correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities with IV fluids as ordered before surgery
Encourage unlimited formula immediately before emergent laparotomy without fluid resuscitation
Prepare for pyloromyotomy after medical stabilization as ordered
Discharge home without evaluation because vomiting is always normal at this age

parameters.text: Serum electrolytes (watch for hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis)

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Lactose intolerance does not produce an olive-like pyloric mass with classic projectile nonbilious pattern of IHPS.
rationales.K2: Correct. Merck/NCBI: IHPS — projectile nonbilious vomiting in early weeks with possible olive mass.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Appendicitis is not the classic 3–6 week olive-mass presentation.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Progressive projectile vomiting with olive mass is not simple overfeeding.
rationales.A1: Incorrect. While NPO pending evaluation may occur, the sourced priority actions are fluid/electrolyte correction and pyloromyotomy after stabilization.
rationales.A2: Correct. Merck: correct dehydration and electrolyte/acid-base abnormalities before pyloromyotomy.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Feeding without correcting fluids/electrolytes and rushing without stabilization is unsafe.
rationales.A4: Correct. Definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy after medical stabilization (Merck/NCBI).
rationales.A5: Incorrect. This presentation requires prompt evaluation, not casual discharge.
rationales.P1: Correct. Dehydration risk is central; monitor hydration/urine output (Merck).
rationales.P2: Correct. Classic abnormality is hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (Merck/NCBI).
rationales.P5: Plausible monitoring but not selected as a keyed parameter for this item; electrolytes and hydration are the highest-yield sourced parameters.
